newsitem.title: FRANCE: Sale plan for Credit Lyonnais not ready.
newsitem.headline: Sale plan for Credit Lyonnais not ready.

text.p: France's privatisation plan for state-controlled bank Credit Lyonnais, which it promised to submit in February to the European Commission for clearance, still is not ready, an official source said on Monday.
The government and Credit Lyonnais have not yet reached agreement on which assets the bank should sell as part of its restructuring, the source said.
"The issue right now is to find a balance that is fair to the shareholder (the state) and to the bank," the source said.

The source said the Commission, which has expressed concern about the amount of public money which has already gone into the bank, was being kept informed about the situation. "There is no problem at that end," the source said.
Briefly the world's biggest bank outside Japan, Credit Lyonnais nearly collapsed in the early 1990s after a lending binge led to massive losses.
The bank which lost 21 billion francs between 1992 and 1994 reported a modest 1996 net profit of 202 million francs and a vastly improved underlying performance.
The talks between the bank and the government have been complicated by Finance Minister Jean Arthuis' unexpected stand that the state would not recapitalise Credit Lyonnais.
He said on Sunday there was "no question of the state taking part in a new recapitalisation."

There had been expectations that the bank, already bailed out twice by the state, would get at least 12 billion francs in state money to boost solvency ratios to ensure its successful privatisation and cover losses on asset sales.
That sum did not include the estimated 15-20 billion franc cost of softening a loan by the bank under a 1995 state rescue to finance the spinoff of dud assets from its balance sheet.

Arthuis's stand, said the source, meant the bank "would have to reduce its field of activity to boost its (solvency) ratio mechanically." Solvency ratios measure the assets of an institution to its liabilities.
Arthuis said he would propose soon to the European Commission, which must approve state aid, that Credit Lyonnais sell "certain, essentially European, businesses."
But many of the bank's assets were bought at the peak of the market and their sale could trigger large capital losses.
The Commission has already indicated it would demand considerable concessions in exchange for approval of the latest plan, including sale of significant Credit Lyonnais activities.

The bank has maintained that a recapitalisation is necessary to pave the way for its privatisation and Credit Lyonnais Jean Peyrelevade has warned the bank cannot endanger its future by selling off strategic operations.
He has hinted he might quit if bank's viability were jeopardised.
Estimates of the total bill for bailing out Credit Lyonnais go as high as 130 billion francs but Arthuis said it was impossible to say what the total cost would be at this stage.
The government has said it aims to privatise the bank in early 1998.
